papers.title: How Many Time-Critical Emergencies? A Population-Based National Estimate of Attended Events per 100,000 US Residents
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo estimate how many time-critical emergencies fire and emergency medical services (EMS) crews attend each year per 100,000 US residents. We counted events in which a crew reached a living patient or a trapped person whose outcome plausibly depends on how soon effective treatment starts. MethodsFor 30 medical conditions, we took annual counts from US registries and datasets, or multiplied a national incidence count by the share of patients EMS attended. A condition was Tier A when a published study linked a measured delay, from minutes to a few hours, to death or major disability. Conditions whose time sensitivity rests on guidelines or expert consensus were Tier B. Fire and rescue events came from twelve months of National Emergency Response Information System public data, scaled to national totals. We removed double counting between conditions. ResultsCrews attended an estimated 589 time-critical events per 100,000 residents a year (494 to 697 with every condition at its low or high value), equal to 4.3% of 9-1-1 EMS activations. Medical conditions accounted for 583 after removing overlap. Of these, 350 were Tier A, led by ischemic stroke (120.2) and EMS-treated cardiac arrest (78.7). Opioid overdose (123.4) led the 233 Tier B events. Those three conditions made up 55% of the medical total. Fire and rescue events added 6. ConclusionsAt national rates, a US community of 100,000 can expect its fire and EMS crews to attend about 589 events a year in which time to treatment may change the outcome. That is roughly 11 a week, nearly all of them medical. The count measures how often response time can matter in the events crews attend, and it gives a denominator for valuing a faster response.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language AI Models Against Human Doctors Using an Emergency Medicine Simulation Approach
papers.abstract: BackgroundProper adoption of AI in emergency medicine necessitate thorough and rigorous appraisal. Classic benchmarks, which rely heavily on basic question-and-answer formats, though dominating the benchmarking field of LLM usage in medicine, have proven inadequate in assessing the full spectrum of skills incumbent upon an agent in healthcare. MethodsWe propose an intricate benchmarking scheme in which the skill set required of an emergency physician is tested and quantified. Our benchmarking structure is 3-fold: skills such as history taking, diagnostic accuracy, treatment plan, and empathy are evaluated by an emergency medicine expert, while the same expertise is scored by an intern from the perspective of a patient, through what we call a simulated emergency room visit. A comprehensive written examination is also utilized to measure general emergency medicine knowledge. ResultsEight LLMs were benchmarked against each other and in contrast to nine emergency medical doctors. Our findings indicate that the AI models significantly outperformed human physicians across several key domains, including history taking, investigation, diagnostic accuracy, and treatment planning. Furthermore, the models demonstrated superior performance in comprehensibility, credibility, and empathy. When comparing AI models against each other, performance advantages were marginal during simulated emergency room visits and were mostly pronounced during the written examination. ConclusionAI models demonstrate a clear advantage over human physicians across a diverse range of emergency medicine competencies. The proposed benchmarking scheme provides a comprehensive metric for a thorough evaluation of medical skill set, furthering validation, adaptation, and utilization of AI in emergency medicine.

papers.title: Diagnosing a cardiac cause for palpitations: Five-year service evaluation of a smartphone ambulatory ECG pathway for Emergency Department patients.
papers.abstract: BackgroundCapturing an electrocardiogram (ECG) during transient symptoms remains challenging in emergency department (ED) patients with palpitations. Following the IPED trial, a smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorder pathway was integrated into NHS care. We evaluated this service over five years, assessing diagnostic yield, management, one-year outcomes and predictors of cardiac arrhythmia. MethodsSingle-centre service evaluation of consecutive patients referred with palpitations to a smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorder clinic between 24th July 2019 and 24th July 2024. Patients underwent event-triggered ECG monitoring using the single-lead Kardia Mobile(R) (AliveCor, Inc.) or their own smartwatch with ECG capability. Clinical characteristics, rhythm recordings, investigation, one-year outcomes and management changes were recorded. Multivarible logistic regression identified independent predictors of one-year cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis. Results1750 patients attended the clinic, mean age 44.3 {+/-} 16.1 years, 58.2% female. 1176 patients (67.2%) underwent monitoring with a cardiac arrhythmia directly captured in 67 patients (5.7% of monitored), including atrial fibrillation (n=39), supraventricular tachycardia (13), atrial flutter (9), atrial tachycardia (5) and ventricular tachycardia (1). By one year, 84 (7.1%) who underwent monitoring received a cardiac diagnosis with 79.8% (67/84) established directly via clinic monitoring. Across the entire cohort (n=1750), 114 (6.5%) had a cardiac cause at one year, 1472 (84.2%) had non-cardiac aetiology and 1569 (89.1%) were discharged back to primary care. Medication changes were initiated in 106 patients (6.1%). Independent predictors of a one-year cardiac diagnosis were increasing age (aOR 1.04 per 1-year increase), prior atrial fibrillation/flutter (aOR 5.57) and a presenting symptom of irregular beating (aOR 2.65). ConclusionOur service provides an effective model for evaluating ED patients with palpitations. Over five years the service reliably detected actionable cardiac arrhythmias while safely discharging nearly 90% of patients to primary care. Clinical characteristics may guide patient selection to maximise clinic efficiency. Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSAlthough the IPED trial established that smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorders improve diagnostic yield for emergency department (ED) patients with palpitations over standard care, data on long-term real-world performance, safety and baseline diagnostic predictors are lacking. What this study addsIn a five-year evaluation of 1750 ED and acute medical unit patients, smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorder monitoring directly established nearly 80% of all 1-year cardiac arrhythmia diagnoses while safely discharging 89% of attendees back to primary care without follow-up. Advancing age, prior atrial fibrillation or flutter, and presenting with irregular beating were independent predictors of a 1-year cardiac diagnosis. How this study might affect research, practice, or policyA smartphone-based ambulatory ECG event recorder clinic is an effective model for evaluating patients with palpitations. Emergency, acute and primary care clinicians can use baseline clinical predictors such as increasing age, cardiac history and a description of irregular beating to prioritise those patients more likely to have an underlying cardiac cause for their palpitations for monitoring and effectively guide local service referral strategies.

papers.title: Dynamic changes in plasma sphingosine-1-phosphate concentrations and mortality in sepsis: a prospective cohort study in the emergency department
papers.abstract: BackgroundSepsis is a dynamic process with evolving host responses, biomarker changes, and organ dysfunction. Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive lipid involved in endothelial and immune regulation. However, the clinical relevance of dynamic S1P changes in sepsis remains unclear. This study aimed to assess their association with mortality. MethodsWe conducted a prospective cohort study of adults recruited from the emergency department of Wan Fang Hospital between April 2022 and October 2024. Plasma S1P was measured by ELISA on days 1, 3, and before discharge or death. The primary outcome was 60-day mortality. S1P trajectories were defined by baseline concentrations and longitudinal slopes estimated using linear mixed-effects models. Low-decreasing, low-stable, and high-decreasing trajectories were grouped as descending; the others as ascending. Cox proportional hazards models assessed mortality associations with baseline S1P, trajectory groups, and time-varying S1P. ResultsAmong 278 participants, 156 had sepsis. Baseline S1P concentrations were lower in patients with sepsis (82.2 [IQR, 47.8-141.1] ng/mL) than in those with non-septic infection (129.2 [IQR, 68.1-306.9] ng/mL) and non-infected controls (132.8 [IQR, 74.1-300.2] ng/mL). In the sepsis cohort, 101 patients were classified into the descending S1P trajectory group and 55 into the ascending group. The descending group had a higher hazard of 60-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 3.43; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.11-10.58; p = 0.032). Baseline S1P was not significantly associated with 60-day mortality (aHR 1.004 per 10 ng/mL decrease; 95% CI, 0.977-1.032; p = 0.803). Each 10 ng/mL decrease in time-varying S1P was associated with a 3.5% higher mortality hazard (aHR 1.035; 95% CI, 1.002-1.076; p = 0.041). ConclusionsDeclining plasma S1P over time was associated with higher mortality in sepsis. Dynamic changes in S1P may be clinically relevant beyond baseline levels.

papers.title: Differences in sepsis from skin and soft tissue infections among patients with vs. without mental health disorders
papers.abstract: IntroductionSepsis is a severe health condition that requires rapid and attentive treatment. The rise in sepsis cases reveals a lack of immediate supportive care in the healthcare system. This lapse may be attributed to a delay in sepsis recognition, patient incompatibility with care plan, and conditions that make treatment more difficult. Building on previous research, this paper seeks to explore the correlation between patients with mental health conditions and sepsis development. State how we define quality of sepsis care. MethodData from 2018-2019 from our ED sepsis quality database was analyzed using T-tests, comparing the characteristics, conditions, and quality of sepsis care of dermatologically-septic patients with and without mental health conditions. ResultsBetween January 1, 2018 and December 31, 2019, 584 LIJ ED patients had sepsis that met inclusion criteria for quality review. Of these, 57 (9.8%) had sepsis of dermatologic origin, of which 30 (52.6%) were female (p = 0.4318). The source of sepsis was the lower extremity in 36.8% of mental health patients vs. 68.4% of non-mental health patients (p = 0.045) and sacral decubitus ulcer in 36.8% of mental health patients vs. 5.3% of non-mental health patients (p = 0.004). In neither univariate nor multivariate analysis were there statistically-significant differences in outcomes in patients with vs. without a mental health issue. However, the need for mechanical ventilation trended lower among patients with mental health disorder (p = 0.141) while the outcome of 3-hour bundle met trended higher among that same group (p = 0.11). DiscussionCompared to patients with mental health issues, those without mental health issues had higher rates of sepsis due to lower extremity infections and sacral decubitus ulcer infections. None of the outcome variables met statistical significance. However, dermatologic sepsis patients without mental health issues tended to be more sick than those with mental health issues, as gauged by rates of septic shock and ICU admission (both trending toward statistical significance). They also trended toward receiving lower quality care, as measured by adherence with the 3-hour sepsis bundle. Failure to achieve statistical significance might be due to the small sample size. This is likely the case, as, for example, there was a substantial difference in the percent of multi-racial patients between those with (5.3%) vs. without (28.9%) mental health illness, yet even this large difference did not meet statistical significance (p = 0.104).

papers.title: Low-risk Features of Emergency Department Patients on a Sepsis Pathway: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: IntroductionFor adult emergency department (ED) patients initiated on a sepsis care pathway, we sought to identify patient factors associated with favorable clinical and operational outcomes that could help identify patients potentially eligible for sepsis care de-escalation. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study using an electronic health record (EHR) data query from five hospitals in New York City (2022-2024). Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate association of patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and ED diagnoses with four favorable reference outcomes: shorter hospital length of stay (HLOS), no intensive care unit (ICU) stay, survival to discharge, and no sepsis adjudication according to institutional quality-of-care standards. ResultsAmong 9,443 ED visits, 45.9% of participants were 36C, absence of hypotension, WBC count 4,000-15,000/uL, and lactate <2.0mmol/L linked to multiple outcomes. Age 18-49 years had the strongest association for HLOS <72 hours (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 3.48, p<0.01) and survival to discharge (aOR 3.15, p<0.01); lack of severe diagnosis had the strongest association for no ICU stay (aOR 2.74, p<0.01); and ED diagnosis other than sepsis or infection had the strongest association for no sepsis adjudication (aOR 8.82, p<0.01). WBC count 4,000/uL to 15,000/uL was the only factor associated with all four outcomes (aORs 1.24-1.70). Patients with a primary ED diagnosis of infection other than pneumonia had more favorable outcomes than those diagnosed with sepsis or pneumonia. ConclusionSeveral patient factors may help identify lower risk patients who could be targeted for sepsis care de-escalation after a sepsis pathway has been initiated, although the relevant factors differ by outcome. Further research is needed to evaluate the performance of these factors in prospectively identifying patients most likely to experience favorable outcomes.

papers.title: Diagnosis, triage and response quality of five large language models on emergency medicine vignettes: a blinded comparison
papers.abstract: BackgroundEmergency care requires appropriate triage and management as well as diagnosis. We compared five large language models on these tasks using the same clinical vignettes. MethodsSeventeen synthetic emergency department vignettes were submitted to Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Grok 4.5, Gemini 3.6 Flash and Kimi K3 through consumer interfaces on 11-12 August 2026. Two emergency physicians independently assessed the 85 responses with model identities concealed. Outcomes were agreement with reference diagnoses and Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) levels, appropriateness and overall quality (1-5 scales), potential harm and preferred response. ResultsEvery model correctly named the reference diagnosis in all 17 cases. CTAS exact agreement ranged from 14/17 to 15/17 per model (p=0.938). Of 13 discordant assignments, nine were undertriage and four overtriage. Appropriateness and quality differed across models (both p<0.001): Kimi K3 had the highest mean scores (4.82 and 4.74) and Grok 4.5 the lowest (3.91 and 3.71); Grok 4.5 scored significantly lower than every other model on both scales after Holm adjustment. Nine responses were flagged for potential harm: four from Grok 4.5, two each from Gemini 3.6 Flash and GPT-5.6 Sol, one from Claude Fable 5 and none from Kimi K3 (p=0.119). ConclusionIn this selected set of synthetic vignettes, all five models correctly named the reference diagnosis, yet undertriage and potentially harmful omissions occurred and response quality differed between models. These findings do not establish any models clinical safety. Key messagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSLarge language models have been evaluated on emergency diagnosis, triage and management, including multi-model comparisons using the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale. What this study addsIn 17 synthetic vignettes, five models all named the reference diagnosis, yet physician ratings differed and triage errors and potential-harm flags remained. How this study might affect research, practice or policyLLMs, once clinically validated, have great promise to improve emergency care. Evaluations of these tools should assess management and urgency, not diagnosis alone. These findings do not establish that any model is safe for clinical use.

papers.title: Comparison of patients diagnosed with intimate partner violence with and without brain injury: Retrospective cross-sectional study in a single, urban, academic health system, 2016-2025.
papers.abstract: BackgroundBrain injury (BI) in people who have experienced intimate partner violence (IPV) is underdiagnosed in health care settings. Our project aims to determine how the prevalence and characteristics of people with documented IPV+BI differ from people with IPV alone. MethodsA retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using electronic health record data at Rush University Medical Center (2016-2025). Adults aged 18 years or older were classified into two groups: IPV with brain injury (IPV+BI) and IPV without brain injury (IPV). Demographics, injury patterns, comorbidities, and pre-diagnosis healthcare utilization between cohorts were compared. ResultsIn 1,329,460 adult patients from 2016 to 2025 seen at Rush, 2,816 were diagnosed with IPV (prevalence = 0.21%). Also, 486 were concomitantly diagnosed with IPV+BI (17.2% of the IPV population). Most (71%) of initial diagnosis documentation occurred in an Emergency Room encounter. Alcohol use disorder, anemia, chronic liver disease, and vascular diseases were more common in the IPV+BI cohort, compared to IPV alone. Prior to diagnosis, the IPV+BI cohort utilized significantly more acute care resources but less ambulatory usage. DiscussionElectronic health record documentation of IPV with and without BI mainly occurred in the Emergency Room and was lower than anticipated. People with IPV+BI were more likely to have certain co-morbidities and were less likely to utilize health resources before diagnosis. The findings, if confirmed utilizing data from multiple health systems in the Chicagoland region, can support work to advance diagnosis and management of IPV+BI. KEYPOINTSO_LIIn 1,329,460 adult patients from 2016 to 2025 seen at Rush, 2,816 were diagnosed with IPV (prevalence = 0.21%) which is lower than reported from public health datasets. C_LIO_LIAlso, 486 were concomitantly diagnosed with IPV+BI (17.2% of the IPV population). C_LIO_LIThe IPV and IPV+BI were initially documented during an emergency room encounter (71% overall, 68% for IPV alone and 93% for IPV+BI) with injury type mainly being unspecified or other head injury rather (74%) rather than traumatic brain injury or strangulation. C_LIO_LIIn the IPV+BI cohort, alcohol use disorder, anemia, chronic liver disease, and vascular diseases were significantly more common than the IPV alone. C_LIO_LIBefore diagnosis, the IPV+BI cohort utilized more acute care but lacked ambulatory usage. C_LI

papers.title: Characteristics, Interventions, and Deprivation Patterns in Suspected Opioid-Associated Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrests Attended by North East Ambulance Service NHS Foundation Trust: A 36-Month Service Evaluation
papers.abstract: BackgroundDrug-poisoning deaths in England and Wales have more than doubled since 2012, with the North East of England persistently reporting the highest mortality rates. Opioid-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OA-OHCA) presents distinct clinical and operational challenges for ambulance services, particularly amid the emergence of potent synthetic opioids and uncertainty over the role of naloxone during cardiac arrest. This service evaluation sought to characterise the incidence, clinical features, and deprivation patterns of suspected OA-OHCA attended by North East Ambulance Service NHS Foundation Trust (NEAS), and to describe their geographic distribution. MethodsA retrospective service evaluation was conducted using structured and reported fields from the NEAS electronic patient care record (ePCR) system between 1 January 2022 and 31 December 2024. Inclusion required a documented cardiac resuscitation together with either a reported aetiology of drug overdose, or documented naloxone administration. Data were analysed descriptively. Results351 cases met the inclusion criteria. The mean age was 42.9 years; 69.2% were male. Cases represented a rising proportion of OHCA where resuscitation was attempted by NEAS across the period (4.7% in 2022 to 5.9% in 2024). Naloxone was administered in 87.2% of incidents, adrenaline in 86.9%, and amiodarone in 9.4%. Advanced airway management was recorded in 88.3% and intraosseous access in 75.5%; defibrillation was performed in 16.5%. Cases were concentrated in the most deprived communities, with Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) deciles 1-3 comprising 71.8% of the cohort. ConclusionSuspected drug-related cardiac arrests in the NEAS region predominantly affected working-age adults in deprived communities, and were managed with consistent airway, ventilation, vascular access, and naloxone administration alongside infrequent defibrillation, consistent with a predominantly asphyxial arrest model. This evaluation provides a descriptive baseline that could inform service planning and provides the empirical foundation for a subsequent qualitative study of paramedic clinical decision-making in OA-OHCA.

papers.title: Are Emergency Departments becoming inaccessible for vulnerable groups of patients? A retrospective cohort study
papers.abstract: BackgroundEmergency Department (ED) overcrowding is associated with adverse outcomes including delays to treatment, patients leaving without being seen and increased mortality. Increasingly, evidence suggests that crowding may disproportionately affect those of lower socioeconomic status, worsening health inequalities. This study investigates the relationship between prolonged ED length of stay and vulnerable patient groups choosing not to wait to be seen. MethodsA retrospective cohort study analysed monthly ED attendance data from a large district general hospital between January 2020 and July 2025. Patients who did not wait to be seen (DNW) were assessed for vulnerability based on age, presenting complaint and inferred frailty. Associations were explored using generalised estimation equation model with binary outcome. ResultsDuring the 66-month study period, 317,978 patients attended the ED, of whom 35,403 (11.1%) did not wait to be seen. Of these, just under one third met vulnerability criteria. As the percentage of patients staying in the ED for more than 8-hours increased, so did the proportion of patients leaving the department without being seen. With each 10% increase in LOS>8h percentage, the odds of any patient choosing not to wait increases by 48% (OR=1.48, 95% CI(1.47 - 1.49), p<0.001). Of the three vulnerability groups assessed, paediatric patients, those presenting with mental health complaints and frailty, frail patients were the most affected when lengths of stay in the ED increased and crowding became a problem (OR=1.73, 95% CI(1.72 - 1.74), p<0.001). ConclusionThese findings demonstrate that while all patient groups are more likely to leave without being seen as crowding worsens, elderly and paediatric patient cohorts are significantly more likely to leave without being seen as crowding worsens. This raises genuine concerns about the accessibility of healthcare, in the presence of crowding, in these vulnerable groups.

papers.title: Return Visits, Admission, and Mortality After Leaving Without Being Seen Among Emergency Department Patients With Behavioral HealthPresentations
papers.abstract: ImportancePatients with behavioral health presentations leave the emergency department (ED) before evaluation more often than other patients, but outcomes after leaving without being seen (LWBS) have not been described in this population. ObjectiveTo compare return visits, admission, and mortality after LWBS vs completed care among behavioral health ED episodes. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsThis retrospective episode-level cohort study used a multisystem deidentified electronic health record database of US health systems (data snapshot June 4, 2026). Participants were patients of all ages with an ED visit and same-day behavioral health diagnosis. Index visits (recorded January 26, 2001 to April 13, 2025) each opened a 30-day episode window; in-window were counted as outcomes, and patients could contribute episodes to either group. Data were analyzed in October 2026. ExposureLWBS (diagnosis code Z53.21 on a date with an ED encounter) vs completed care ending in discharge home. Main Outcomes and MeasuresThe primary outcome was ED return visit within 7 days. Secondary outcomes were return visit within 3 and 30 days; admission on day 0, on days 1-7 (principal measure), and within 30 days; and all-cause death within 7 and 30 days, assessed among episodes from 2017 through 2023 using a verified death-record definition. ResultsThe analysis included 1,305,812 episodes (12,248 LWBS; 1,293,564 completed care) from 525,490 patients; 666,930 episodes (51.1%) involved female patients and 66,733 (5.1%) involved patients younger than 18 years. Return visit within 7 days followed 24.5% of LWBS episodes vs 13.2% of completed-care episodes (risk ratio [RR], 1.86; 95% CI, 1.81-1.92), and admission on days 1-7 followed 17.1% vs 3.9% (RR, 4.41; 95% CI, 4.24-4.59). Among 2017-2023 episodes, 30-day mortality was 0.69% (70 of 10,141) after LWBS vs 0.32% (2,426 of 756,140) after completed care (RR, 2.15; 95% CI, 1.70-2.73). Results were similar under alternative episode definitions. Conclusions and RelevanceAmong patients with behavioral health ED presentations, LWBS was followed by higher rates of return visits, admission, and short-term mortality than completed care. These unadjusted findings describe outcome burden, not causal effects, and highlight patients who leave as a target for rapid follow-up.

papers.title: Mortality in Rural and Urban Emergency and Trauma Care in the United States: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: ObjectiveRural hospitals in the United States have fewer specialists, fewer critical care resources, and longer transport distances than urban hospitals, yet national studies disagree on whether rural patients are more likely to die after emergency care. The goal of this study was to determine whether short-term mortality differs between rural and urban patients receiving emergency or trauma care and to estimate the size of the difference. MethodsWe conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis reported in line with PRISMA 2020. PubMed was searched on October 11, 2026, for studies published from 2010 onward, supplemented by web searching. Eligible studies were US observational studies that compared rural with urban patients or hospitals and reported mortality after emergency or trauma care. Odds ratios (ORs) were pooled with a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model, with Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals (CIs) as a sensitivity analysis. Injury and trauma studies formed the primary analysis. Certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE. ResultsOf 161 records identified, 14 studies were included and 12 were pooled. Across seven injury and trauma studies, rural setting was associated with higher odds of death (OR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.07-1.52), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 84%; 95% prediction interval, 0.74-2.19). Across all 12 studies, the pooled OR was 1.23 (95% CI, 1.09-1.40; I2 = 96%). With Hartung-Knapp intervals, the overall estimate remained significant (95% CI, 1.05-1.45) and the trauma estimate was borderline (95% CI, 0.99-1.64). Study estimates ranged from 0.65 to 1.97. Three pediatric trauma studies gave a consistent estimate (OR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.18-1.47; I2 = 0%). Subgroup analyses by rurality definition, age group, and geographic scope did not explain the heterogeneity. Certainty of evidence was very low. ConclusionsIn pooled US observational data, rural patients receiving emergency and trauma care had about 23% higher odds of short-term death than urban patients, most consistently among injured children. The evidence is inconsistent, rests on a single-database search with several reports assessed from abstracts only, and should be treated as preliminary. Why rural patients die more often, and at what point in the pathway from injury to definitive care, remains unanswered.

papers.title: Performance of the Heatwave ED Forecast Tool in the Emergency Department Network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland
papers.abstract: ObjectivesHeatwaves drive surges in acute care demand, yet heat-health action plans (HHAPs) lack tools to scale emergency care responses. This study validated a forecasting tool for heatwave- related emergency department (ED) demand across four clusters comprising the emergency care network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland. MethodsThis retrospective, ecological, time-series study modeled daily mean temperature and ED presentations using a distributed lag non-linear model framework with autoregressive and calendar adjustment components. The model was trained on summers (June-August) 2016-2024 and tested on summer 2025, defining heatwaves as daily mean temperature >25 {degrees}C for [≥]3 consecutive days. ResultsA non-linear temperature-demand association was shown across the clusters, with ED visits increasing at higher temperatures. Model fit varied across clusters (R{superscript 2} 0.389-0.672), and the reference model consistently outperformed naive baselines. During two heatwaves in 2025, prediction errors remained within acceptable ranges. Baseline demand, heatwave occurrence, and model performance varied substantially within the canton. ConclusionsThese findings have implications for the design of HHAPs, suggesting that emergency care preparedness should rely on locally calibrated demand forecast rather than standardized activation protocols.

papers.title: SCORES (Selection of Clinical Observations for Risk Evaluation Scores): Impact of Heart Rate Selection on Simplified Geneva Score Performance in Suspected Pulmonary Embolism
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe Simplified Geneva Score (SGS) incorporates two heart-rate thresholds. Multiple heart-rate measurements are commonly recorded during emergency department (ED) assessment. While the original SGS specifies use of mean heart rate, real-world implementation is unlikely to reflect this, and the effect of alternative heart-rate selection methods on score performance is unknown. MethodsSCORES was a retrospective within-subject study of consecutive ED patients at a single urban hospital undergoing computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for suspected pulmonary embolism (PE). Four SGS variants were calculated using the first, highest, mean, and lowest recorded pre-CTPA heart rate. Outcomes included score output, risk classification, diagnostic performance, reclassification flow, and downstream imaging utilisation. Precision estimates and comparisons were derived using empirical resampling techniques. Results590 episodes were reviewed with 581 included for analysis. PE was confirmed in 50 cases (8.6%). Mean SGS differed significantly across all heart-rate implementations (p<0.0001). The proportion classified as high risk varied from 15% using the lowest heart rate to 40% using the highest heart rate. Reclassification across the SGS threshold was common, with 25% of episodes changing risk category unidirectionally between lowest and highest heart rate implementations. SGS(lowest HR) compared with SGS(mean HR) and SGS(highest HR) demonstrated higher specificity (87.6% vs 73.4% vs 62.1%), improved AUROC (0.744 vs 0.704 vs 0.659), and reduced downstream CTPA utilisation (818 vs 876 vs 920 scans per 100 PEs diagnosed), with no additional pulmonary emboli missed within the complete diagnostic pathway. ConclusionsHeart-rate selection materially influences SGS output, risk classification, diagnostic performance, and imaging utilisation. In this retrospective cohort, use of the lowest recorded heart rate produced the most favourable overall balance of discrimination and diagnostic efficiency, supporting prospective validation.

papers.title: Protocol and Statistical Analysis Plan for the Waveform Capnography versus Colorimetric Carbon Dioxide Detection During Tracheal Intubation of Critically Ill Adults (WAVE) Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundDuring emergency tracheal intubation, clinicians use waveform capnography or colorimetric carbon dioxide (CO2) detection to confirm exhaled CO2 from the endotracheal tube to determine its location. Both devices reliably yield a negative result when the tube is in the esophagus. However, in most emergency intubations the tube is correctly located in the trachea, and in this circumstance the relative diagnostic accuracy of the two devices is uncertain. If one device more often fails to detect exhaled CO2 despite correct tube placement (a false negative result), this could lead to unnecessary tube removal, repeated intubation attempts, and an increased risk of serious complications. Research QuestionAmong critically ill adults undergoing emergency tracheal intubation, is waveform capnography or colorimetric CO2 detection more sensitive for identifying an endotracheal tube correctly placed in the trachea? Study Design and MethodsThe WAVE study is a pragmatic, prospective, paired diagnostic accuracy study conducted in emergency departments and intensive care units in the United States. The study compares waveform capnography and colorimetric CO2 detection (index tests) against a non-CO2-based reference standard for endotracheal tube location among 2,092 critically ill adults undergoing tracheal intubation. The primary outcome is the sensitivity of each index test for identifying a tube located in the trachea. The secondary outcome is specificity for identifying a tube located outside the trachea. ResultsEnrollment began on April 21, 2025 and is ongoing, with completion anticipated in 2026. InterpretationThe WAVE study will provide prospective evidence comparing waveform capnography with colorimetric CO2 detection for determination of endotracheal tube location in critically ill adults. These findings may inform clinical practice and guideline recommendations regarding the optimal test of exhaled CO2 for use in the ED and ICU. Prespecifying the protocol and statistical analysis plan before completion of enrollment enhances the rigor, reproducibility, and transparency of the study.

papers.title: Factors associated with discharge and return visits of emergency department patients with a sepsis best practice alert
papers.abstract: BackgroundBest practice alerts (BPAs) used in emergency departments (EDs) to identify patients with possible sepsis lack specificity and some ED patients with sepsis BPAs are discharged. We evaluated factors associated with ED discharge following a sepsis BPA and with subsequent 7-day return admissions with sepsis or infection. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study using an electronic health record data query from five hospitals (2022-2024). Using logistic regression, we evaluated the association of participant demographics and clinical characteristics with ED discharge and factors at the initial ED visit associated with return admission. ResultsAmong 62,068 ED visits with a sepsis BPA, one third resulted in ED discharge. Discharged participants were younger and more often female, Black, multiracial, and/or Hispanic; they more often had an initially normal pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and lactic acid than admitted participants. Discharged participants more often had a fever on arrival (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 6.03; p<0.001) and a white blood cell (WBC) count 11,000-14,999 (aOR 4.57; p<0.001) or 15,000-19,999/uL (aOR 2.01; p<0.001). One percent of discharged participants experienced a 7-day return admission with a diagnosis of sepsis or infection, which was associated with older age, White or Asian race, diastolic hypotension, WBC count [≤]15,000/uL or <4,000/uL, and an index visit BPA response indicating sepsis or non-response. ConclusionsReturn admissions among discharged ED patients with a sepsis BPA are rare. Several factors are associated both with hospital admission at the index visit and return admission, indicating a need for additional risk-stratification tools.

papers.title: Learning the electronic health record at the minute-scale
papers.abstract: Electronic health record foundation models are traditionally trained on the scale of years, days, or hours. These timescales, however, lack the minute-scale resolution required to directly guide clinical decisions at the bedside. We introduced minute-scale learning, a new paradigm for training and evaluating models, and developed MINT, a minute-scale foundation model for pediatric emergencies. MINT was pretrained and validated on 766,733 pediatric emergency department visits at five health systems, comprising 16 years of data from 10 hospitals. On minute-scale forecasting tasks, MINT outperformed and generalized to external health systems better than task-specific models (superior in 21 of 25 comparisons). MINT outperformed physicians in forecasting escalations of respiratory support. MINT demonstrated uniquely minute-scale capabilities including department-scale monitoring, dynamic risk explanations, individualized physiologic response forecasts, and hypothesis generation. Learning at the minute-scale improves performance, strengthens generalizability, and provides insights, actionability, and scientific capabilities that are not accessible at other timescales.

papers.title: Healthcare providers perceptions of barriers and facilitators to implementation of an acute traumatic brain injury clinical practice guideline: a CFIR-informed qualitative study at a regional referral hospital in Northern Tanzania
papers.abstract: BackgroundTraumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), where the burden of injury is disproportionately high, and healthcare resources are often limited. Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) improve the consistency and quality of TBI care by shifting medical decision-making from individual judgement to evidence-based recommendations. The strong link between improved TBI outcomes and CPG adoption has largely been established in high-income country (HIC) hospital settings; evidence on implementing TBI CPGs in LMIC hospital settings is limited. ObjectiveThis study explored healthcare providers experiences to identify barriers and facilitators to implementing a TBI CPG in the Emergency Department (EMD) at Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Center in Northern Tanzania, guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research 2.0 (CFIR). MethodsWe conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews (IDIs) with doctors and nurses who regularly managed TBI patients at the EMD. We purposively sampled participants between June and August 2023. The research team analysed data using thematic content analysis guided by CFIR domains, developing codes and memos iteratively. Results7 nurses and 8 doctors with an average of 5 years of experience caring for patients in the EMD completed in-person, in-depth interviews. Most providers reported frequent exposure to TBI cases and regular use of the CPG in routine clinical practice. However, not all participants reported consistent CPG use, highlighting variation in implementation among providers. Key facilitators included strong interprofessional teamwork, readily accessible guideline materials in clinical areas, availability of diagnostic imaging, and perceived improvements in patient outcomes. Barriers to consistent adherence included ICU bed shortages, limited operating theatre capacity, equipment and medication stock-outs, high patient volumes, staffing pressures, and a lack of structured refresher training or formal audit and feedback mechanisms. Variability in procedural confidence, particularly among less experienced providers, also affected implementation consistency. ConclusionOur findings show that a TBI CPG is well accepted and largely integrated into routine care among experienced providers. However, sustainability depends on strengthening training, mentorship, audit, and feedback systems for CPG use and on addressing system-level resource constraints. Institutional investment in capacity building is essential to ensure consistent and sustained CPG uptake in our setting.

papers.title: Chest Pain Hospitalizations: How Varying Emergency Clinician Tendencies Impact Care, Outcomes, and Costs
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe practice of hospitalizing emergency department (ED) patients with chest pain after ruling out acute myocardial infarction (AMI) varies widely. The long-term outcome and cost implications of this variation are uncertain. MethodsAnalyzing 2007-2021 claims from a national commercial insurer, we identified 223,569 adults ([≥]18 years) ED visits with a principal diagnosis of chest pain without major secondary cardiopulmonary diagnoses, seen by 19,001 clinicians in 2,273 EDs. Within each ED, clinicians with the highest and lowest terciles of risk-adjusted hospitalization rates were classified as high-versus low-admitting. Primary outcomes were 30-and 180-day subsequent AMI hospitalizations. Secondary outcomes included 7-day cardiac testing, 30-day coronary intervention, and 30-day total and out-of-pocket costs. We estimated adjusted rate ratios (aRRs) and relative cost differences using generalized estimating equations, adjusting for patient and visit characteristics. ResultsPatients had a mean age of 48.6 years, and 53.9% were female; measured characteristics were similar between groups. Compared with low-admitting clinicians, visits to high-admitting clinicians had higher 7-day cardiac testing (13.1% vs 10.8%; aRR 1.22, 95% CI 1.17-1.27) and 30-day coronary interventions (4.3% vs 3.8%; aRR 1.16, 95% CI 1.09-1.23). AMI hospitalization did not differ at 30 days (0.60% vs 0.60%; aRR 1.00, 95% CI 0.84-1.15) or 180 days (0.85% vs 0.87%; aRR 0.97, 95% CI 0.85-1.10). Thirty-day total costs were higher after visits to high-admitting clinicians (relative change 11.3%, 95% CI 8.8-13.8), and out-of-pocket costs [≥]$1,000 were more common (32.0% vs 29.6%; relative change 8.2%, 95% CI 6.1-10.3). ConclusionsHigher clinician hospitalizing tendency for ED chest pain is associated with greater downstream testing, more coronary interventions, and higher costs without lower short-or intermediate-term AMI risk. Reducing marginal admissions among high-admitting clinicians may decrease spending and practice variation with minimal impact on AMI outcomes.

papers.title: Quality, Readability, and Content Deficiencies of Three Large Language Models in Bee Sting Health Information: A Comparative Evaluation with Patient Perspectives
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the information quality, reliability, readability, and content deficits of ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao in answering frequently asked questions about bee stings. MethodsTwenty-five high-frequency patient questions were selected based on Google Trends, domestic health platforms, and allergy guidelines, and submitted to the three LLMs, yielding 75 responses. Two emergency physicians independently assessed quality using GQS, mDISCERN, QAMAI, EQIP, and PEMAT-U/A. Readability was evaluated using six indices (ARI, FRES, GFI, FKGL, CLI, SMOG). Content deficits were classified qualitatively. Twenty emergency department patients evaluated the comprehensibility and credibility of AI responses. ResultsSignificant differences were found among the three models on all quality metrics (all P < 0.01). DeepSeek achieved the highest mDISCERN score (median 21.00); ChatGPT led on QAMAI (25.00) and EQIP (75.00%); Doubao ranked lowest on all quality indicators but highest on PEMAT-U (73.00%). No model met the sixth-grade reading level standard. Eleven content deficits were identified: outdated medical advice (45.45%), omissions (36.36%), and hallucinations (18.18%). Doubao received the highest patient preference (45.0%). ConclusionThe three LLMs exhibited distinct strengths: DeepSeek in source reliability, ChatGPT in overall quality, and Doubao in understandability. All models had excessively high readability levels, and outdated medical advice was the predominant content deficit.

papers.title: Health system transitions and engagement for patients with opioid use disorder
papers.abstract: BackgroundOpioid Use Disorder (OUD) imposes a rising mortality and health system burden, with opioid-related deaths increasing from 8,400 in 2000 to 110,037 in 2023. Medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) reduce mortality and morbidity, yet only 25.1% of people with OUD are treated with these medications, and inpatient MOUD initiation is inconsistent. Inpatient and Emergency Department (ED) treatment initiation and connection to outpatient care is suboptimal, missing critical opportunities to engage at-risk populations during acute care visits. Our goals were to determine the proportion of patients with OUD treated with MOUD during a hospital/ED stay, and the proportion successfully connected to outpatient care. MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included patients [≥]18 years with an OUD diagnosis at Duke University Hospital and Duke Regional Hospital (7/1/2023-12/31/2025) who had an inpatient or ED encounter with an associated OUD diagnosis code. Primary outcomes were buprenorphine at discharge, 30-day acute care return, and 30-day outpatient follow-up. Adjusted modified Poisson regression models with cluster-robust standard errors evaluated associations with age, sex, race/ethnicity, insurance, area deprivation index, encounter type, and comorbidity score. ResultsOf 5,390 patients with OUD, 42.1% (2,267) had an acute care encounter, generating 3,893 encounters. Neither buprenorphine nor methadone was prescribed at discharge for 46.0% of encounters. Acute care return occurred in 33.6% and outpatient follow-up in 32.2% of encounters within 30 days; only 7.4% of follow-ups included a buprenorphine prescription. ED encounters had lower discharge prescribing than inpatient encounters (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.61-0.86). Black patients had higher 30-day acute care return than White patients (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.02-1.30) ConclusionsAcute care encounters represent repeated, missed opportunities for MOUD initiation. Disparities were concentrated in post-discharge return and follow-up rather than at initial prescribing, and attrition occurred at each transition along the screening-treatment-referral pathway.

papers.title: A Modeling Analysis of Strategies for Allocating Emergency Department HIV and Syphilis Screening Funds in California
papers.abstract: IntroductionUsing an open enrollment process in 2023, California funded 28 emergency departments (EDs) to implement or expand HIV and syphilis screening programs. Californias 2026 state budget now commits an additional $60 million, over six years, to renew support for this screening. How renewed funds are allocated will determine which communities they reach. This analysis establishes a framework derived from public information to simulate and compare several funding strategies, highlighting the tradeoffs across disease burden, geographic reach, and social vulnerability. MethodsPublicly available data were used to construct ED-level profiles for the 282 EDs in the 35 California counties with populations exceeding 100,000. Profiles were then linked to corresponding HIV and syphilis burden (z-score), measures of social vulnerability for the surrounding service area , and socioeconomic and demographic characteristics of the population each ED serves. At a 28 ED award scale, allocation strategies (random selection, prior 2023 awardees, federal priority-county targeting, ranking on burden alone, and a composite of burden, vulnerability, and visit volume) were then compared, simulating ED participation across 100,000 Monte Carlo draws at 70% participation. Sensitivity analyses included varied (50% and 90%) participation and a larger (n=64) ED award scale. Analyses were conducted in 2026. ResultsNo single strategy performed best. Ranking on burden alone reached the highest mean county burden but only 4 of 35 counties, whereas a composite approach reached 8 counties, the highest social vulnerability, and the largest share of patients who identified as Hispanic. Every targeted strategy performed better than both random selection and the prior 2023 awardees on burden but reached fewer counties than either. In sensitivity analyses, the tradeoffs between burden and reach persisted across participation rates and at the 64-ED scale.

papers.title: Analysing dispatch decision making in high-complexity environments: The P.A.T.H.S. framework
papers.abstract: BackgroundDecision-making in emergency services involving the allocation of scarce resources is a key challenge for large, complex organisations required to prioritise demand against multiple, often competing criteria. Emergency Medical Dispatch is a case in point, where Enhanced and Critical Care Teams (ECCTs) represent a scarce and lifesaving clinical resource. Despite its operational and system-level significance, the allocation of ECCTs remains under-researched. MethodsWe conducted a methodological development study using the P.A.T.H.S. framework (Participants, Artefacts, Transition Stages, Historicity, Setting). We designed and piloted this in our previous work under the 999 R.E.S.P.O.N.D. project, which examined the decision-making process for ECCT dispatch. We applied P.A.T.H.S. to 17 dispatch cases (comprising 100 decision-making episodes). We analysed five data sources: recordings of emergency calls and internal dispatch-related interactions, sequence-of-events records, policy documents, and ethnographic observations. A four-phase analysis--indexing & data mapping, transcription & coding, charting, and synthesising & outputs--was undertaken taking Interactional Sociolinguistics as the theoretical approach and methodology. ResultsP.A.T.H.S. enables the mapping of non-linear, multifactorial textual trajectories across human and non-human actors. The case example presented herein illustrates how information on key risk indicators (e.g. mechanism of injury) were often delayed, fragmented, or lost between the caller, call-handler, and written records. P.A.T.H.S. provides a framework and analytical tool capturing the textual trajectory of information flow, and trace how dispatch decision making unfolds. We subsequently developed a template and codebook for other researchers to further study complex decision making in multi-actoral systems using a textual trajectory approach. ConclusionThis methodological development work demonstrates the potential of P.A.T.H.S. to capture and clarify complex decision-making processes. P.A.T.H.S. offers a practical and theoretically grounded framework for future research, training, and policy that addresses risk points in communication between oral and written forms among teams of actors, to support optimal deployment of scarce resources.

papers.title: Acutelines: a Dutch emergency department-based data-biobank for multimodal, longitudinal acute care research
papers.abstract: BackgroundHigh-quality, longitudinal data from the Emergency Department (ED) are essential for understanding acute illness trajectories and for developing clinically deployable prediction models. However, most existing ED datasets are static, limited in modality or disconnected from long-term outcomes or biomaterials. MethodsWe describe a two-year sample of Acutelines, a continuously operating ED-based data-biobank infrastructure at the University Medical Center Groningen. Acutelines is embedded in routine care and captures the full acute care trajectory and uses a stepped consent procedure. It integrates demographics, vital signs, laboratory results, diagnoses, treatments, waveforms, patient-reported outcomes, and prospectively collected biomaterials. Data are linked to in-hospital outcomes and post-discharge mortality. ResultsThe presented dataset comprises 29,314 ED visits from 18,850 adult patients. Clinical variables are available for nearly all visits, with additional data and questionnaires (n=4,963) and biomaterials (n=2,723) collected in predefined subgroups. Associations between early triage features (National Early Warning Score, vital signs, diagnostic categories) and outcomes, illustrate the clinical depth and longitudinal value of the infrastructure. ConclusionAcutelines is a living, continuously expanding research infrastructure. Its combination of ED-first inclusion, multimodal data, linkage to long-term outcomes, and availability of biomaterials distinguishes it from existing datasets. Acutelines provides a robust foundation for hypothesis generation, translational research, and the development, validation, and benchmarking of data-driven clinical decision support tools and biomarker tests in acute medicine, while its ongoing expansion enables prospective studies and interventional research. Trial registrationAcutelines is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov under trial registration number NCT04615065.

papers.title: Ambulance or corridor? The association between site-level use of ambulance 'ramping as Emergency Department escalation areas and 28-day mortality in admitted patients: a secondary analysis of the UNCORKED study
papers.abstract: Background and importanceEmergency Department (ED) crowding is an increasing public health concern, with evidence of harms to patients, the public and healthcare systems. When the number of patients requiring emergency care exceeds the capacity of EDs, operational decisions must be made regarding the best place of care for patients. It is not known if there is an association between place of escalation area care (for example ramping in an ambulance, or in an ED corridor) and patient outcomes. Objective(s)This study aimed to assess the association between the relative proportion of all escalation area care that a site provided in an ambulance (the Ambulance:Escalation Index) and all-cause 28-day mortality. DesignA secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study. Adult patients [≥]16 years attending EDs in England, Wales and Northern Ireland in March 2025. Intervention or exposure (if any)The Ambulance:Escalation Index, a site-level indicator of the proportion of all time in escalation area care provided in an ambulance. Outcome measures and analysisThe profile of site-level ambulance use was presented descriptively. Multivariable survival analysis was used to assess the primary outcome, all-cause 28-day mortality. Main resultsOf 131 EDs using escalation area, 82 (62.6%) used ambulances as a place of escalation area care. There was a significant association between a sites increasing use of ambulances as escalation areas and mortality; for each 5% increase in the proportion of a sites total escalation area care delivered in ambulances, there was a 2.1% increase in the hazard of death by 28 days (HR 1.021, 95% CI 1.002-1.041, p=0.032). ConclusionEmergency Department crowding is associated with poor outcomes irrespective of where departments are forced to deliver care; however this study suggests that there is excess mortality where escalation area care is more often delivered in ambulances.

papers.title: Analytical Performance and 99th Percentile Upper Reference Limit of the Novel SPINCHIP High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin I Point-of-Care Assay
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDIn line with International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) recommendations for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin assays, analytical validation and reference limit assessments are required to confirm that an assay meets performance criteria. This study evaluated the analytical performance and established the 99th percentile upper reference limit (URL) for the SPINCHIP(R) High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin I ("SPINCHIP hs-cTnI") point-of-care assay. METHODSAnalytical performance characteristics, including the limit of blank (LoB), limit of detection (LoD), and limit of quantification (LoQ), were assessed. Additionally, 1053 plasma samples and 1055 whole-blood samples were used to determine the URL. Imprecision around the 99th percentile URL was evaluated as part of the analytical validation. High-sensitivity criteria were assessed by confirming measurable cTnI in [≥]50% of healthy individuals (n=432 plasma; n=431 whole blood) and achieving imprecision <10% at the 99th percentile (plasma, n=960; whole blood, n=480). RESULTSSPINCHIP hs-cTnI demonstrated a LoB of 0.3 ng/L; LoDs of 0.8 ng/L (plasma) and 0.9 ng/L (whole blood); and LoQs of 1.1 ng/L (plasma) and 1.4 ng/L (whole blood). The analytical measuring range was 1.1-9000 ng/L. Imprecision at the common 99th percentile URL (14 ng/L) was 5.8%; for men (URL=16 ng/L) 5.6% and for women (URL=10 ng/L) 6.3%. Greater than 85.2% (94.0% and 76.1% in men and women, respectively) of healthy individuals showed measurable cTnI above the LoD. CONCLUSIONSThe SPINCHIP hs-cTnI assay meets the IFCC high-sensitivity requirements, demonstrating <10% imprecision at the 99th percentile, reliable low-concentration precision. and cTnI detection in more than half of healthy individuals. IMPACT STATEMENTHigh-sensitivity cardiac troponin assays must demonstrate exceptional analytical rigor to ensure clinicians can rely on them for timely and accurate detection of myocardial injury. This study provides a comprehensive analytical validation of the SPINCHIP(R) hs-cTnI point-of-care assay to confirm that it meets key International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine high-sensitivity criteria, including precise quantification at the 99th percentile and detection of measurable cardiac troponin concentrations in the majority of healthy individuals. These findings establish the assays analytical robustness and support its potential to deliver rapid, trustworthy cardiac troponin results at the point-of-care, helping streamline clinical decision making where speed and accuracy are critical.

papers.title: External validation of a decision rule for bacteremia vs contaminants in pediatric blood cultures
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDHalf of positive blood cultures in pediatric emergency departments (PEDs) represent contaminants, driving unnecessary hospitalization, antibiotic exposure, and repeat visits. A clinical decision rule derived at CHU Sainte-Justine showed 99% sensitivity and 60% specificity for distinguishing bacteremia from contaminants but had not been externally validated. We sought to validate this rule in an independent pediatric cohort. METHODSThis retrospective diagnostic study spanned from January 2015 to May 2025 at a tertiary PED in Switzerland, using positive blood cultures from patients younger than 16 years. The four predictors (Gram-negative organisms or Gram-positive cocci in pairs or chains; time to positivity <17 hours; indwelling device; suspected osteoarticular infection) classified each case as low, moderate, or high risk. The primary outcome was bacteremia, adjudicated by two independent reviewers, based on organism identity and infectious disease specialists assessment. Diagnostic accuracy was assessed with 95% CIs. RESULTSOf 130 children enrolled (median age 3.8 years [IQR 0.9-9.9]; 61.5% male), 78 (60.0%) had true bacteremia. The rule yielded a sensitivity of 97.4% (95% CI, 91.0-99.7), specificity of 69.2% (95% CI, 54.9-81.3), positive predictive value of 82.6% (95% CI, 73.3-89.7), and negative predictive value of 94.7% (95% CI, 82.3-99.4). Both false-negatives were immunocompetent children with methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia without indwelling devices. Among contaminants, 71% received antibiotics under usual care versus 31% classified as moderate or high risk by the rule. CONCLUSIONSThis first external validation supports the Sainte-Justine rule in a distinct pediatric population, preserving sensitivity with higher specificity. Multicenter validation is warranted before adoption.

papers.title: Chronic disease burden, not admission laboratory results, marks limb-threatening severity in acute lower-limb arterial thrombosis: a registry study of 288 patients from Kazakhstan
papers.abstract: Acute lower-limb arterial thrombosis is a vascular emergency that often reaches internists and emergency physicians before a vascular specialist, and data from Central Asia are scarce. We asked which patient-level factors mark limb-threatening severity at first presentation, and whether routine admission laboratory tests add to that judgement. We studied a registry of 288 consecutive patients hospitalised with acute lower-limb arterial thrombosis between 2017 and 2022 at a tertiary centre in Karaganda, Kazakhstan. Severity was graded with the Savelyev classification, with grades IIB-IIIA defined as limb-threatening. Associations were tested by logistic regression with Firth-penalised and bootstrap sensitivity analyses, and predictors of tissue loss were modelled separately. Patients were mostly elderly men (median age 67 years, 72.2% male) with a heavy atherosclerotic burden (hypertension 74.0%, coronary disease 54.9%, diabetes 19.1%, prior lower-limb revascularisation 21.2% open and 14.6% endovascular). At presentation 142 (49.3%) had limb-threatening ischaemia and 31 (10.8%) tissue loss. Independent markers of limb-threatening severity were diabetes (adjusted odds ratio 2.15, 95% CI 1.02-4.55), hypertension (2.14, 1.05-4.37), tissue loss (2.55, 1.01-6.45) and lower body-mass index (0.71 per 5 kg/m{superscript 2}, 0.52-0.97). Admission haematology, coagulation and metabolic values did not differ between severity groups (all p>0.05), and the chronic-disease model discriminated modestly (area under the curve 0.68). Low body-mass index (0.49 per 5 kg/m{superscript 2}, p=0.005) and prior amputation (7.08, p=0.04) independently predicted tissue loss. In this cross-sectional analysis, limb-threatening severity was associated with the chronic vascular-metabolic phenotype rather than with the measured admission laboratory profile, which did not separate the severity groups; a leucocyte differential was not recorded, so the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio could not be assessed. Low body weight was a consistent marker of more severe disease. At first contact the severity signal sat with the bedside assessment rather than the routine admission bloods examined here, a pattern that needs prospective testing.

papers.title: Projecting EMS Workforce Demand in an Aging State: A Florida Forecast Through 2035
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVESPopulation aging is a major contributor to increasing demand for emergency medical services (EMS), yet EMS workforce projections based on population data remain limited. This study projected future EMS incident volume and clinician workforce requirements in Florida from 2026 to 2035 based on historical data on EMS response records to inform workforce planning. METHODSWe conducted a retrospective, population-based secondary analysis and forecasting study using de-identified state-wide emergency EMS response records from Floridas Emergency Medical Services Tracking and Reporting System (EMSTARS) spanning January 1, 2017 through December 31, 2025. Incidents were assigned to seven age cohorts and aggregated into monthly time series. We used Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average models with exogenous inputs (SARIMAX) to project age and cohort-specific incident volume for 2026 through 2035. Projected future incident volumes were translated into EMT and paramedic full-time equivalent (FTE) requirements using observed EMSTARS staffing configurations and target operational parameters. RESULTSAnnual EMS incidents increased from 4.10 million in 2017 to 5.22 million in 2025 and are projected to reach 7.76 million by 2035, a 48.8% increase over the 2025 baseline. By 2035, adults aged 60 and older are projected to represent 31.2% of Floridas population while accounting for 61.6% of all EMS incidents. Total estimated EMS workforce requirements are projected to increase from 9,542 FTEs in 2025 to 14,195 FTEs by 2035, requiring approximately 4,654 additional FTEs (a 48.8% increase). CONCLUSIONSFloridas aging population is projected to drive a nearly 50% increase in EMS incident volume and associated workforce requirements over the next decade, with demand disproportionately concentrated among older adults. With a substantial concentration of adults aged 80 and older and a rapidly expanding oldest-old cohort, Florida is confronting the demographic conditions projected to emerge in other states over the next decade. The findings offer researchers and policymakers a replicable framework and a directly applicable planning reference for jurisdictions across the United States.

papers.title: Early Joint Trajectories of Liver-Related Laboratory Biomarkers and 60-Day Mortality in Sepsis-Associated Liver Injury
papers.abstract: BackgroundSepsis-associated liver injury (SALI) is commonly assessed using static laboratory values, although liver dysfunction during sepsis is dynamic. MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included 162 ICU patients with SALI. Early trajectories of alanine aminotransferase, total bilirubin, and albumin during the first 7 days after ICU admission were identified using group-based multi-trajectory modeling. Landmark analysis and Cox regression were used to evaluate 60-day mortality. ResultsTwenty-five patients died within 60 days. Four trajectory classes were identified. Between-class separation was driven mainly by alanine aminotransferase and total bilirubin, whereas albumin showed limited short-term variation. After the landmark time point, Class 3 (HR, 4.374; 95% CI, 1.960-9.759; P <0 .001) and Class 4 (HR, 7.451; 95% CI, 3.649-15.212; P <0 .001) had higher mortality risk than Class 1. ConclusionsEarly joint trajectories of liver-related laboratory biomarkers may identify clinically meaningful SALI subphenotypes and support risk stratification in critically ill patients.
